pending_qa.q: How is the role of legal expertise evolving in real estate transaction negotiations?
pending_qa.r: Brokers and owners now demand a higher level of expertise from lawyers and legal staff because AI tools like ChatGPT and Claude can proof documents, but what lawyers uniquely provide is deal advice—understanding market context, identifying long-term concerns, and knowing when to push. The profession is increasingly becoming an emotionally intelligent game focused on negotiation and relationship dynamics rather than just code knowledge, as emotional intelligence combined with artificial intelligence application is the future of the next 10 years.

pending_qa.q: What limitations exist when relying solely on artificial intelligence for property valuation in commercial real estate?
pending_qa.r: AI is ultimately programmed to keep users invested rather than seek objective truth; in one deal, AI told Gordon's client a property was worth a certain amount, but when they role-played as the landlord, AI simply told the landlord what they wanted to hear instead. Brokers must understand that AI is a great resource but not absolute truth, and humans with broker licenses and market expertise must verify AI recommendations against actual market conditions and feasibility to find a true meeting of the minds.

pending_qa.q: How does a broker's client selection process change as their track record and reputation grow?
pending_qa.r: As Gordon became more successful, he went from accepting nearly every potential client to receiving two or three inquiries per day and having to select which deals to pursue. Most weeks he turns down more people than he accepts because to consistently execute 100-plus transactions annually, deals must be real opportunities with closable buyers or realistic sellers, creditworthy tenants with genuine business plans; evaluating a prospect's website, business background, credit history, and current space in 15-20 minutes helps identify which opportunities are worth pursuing versus time-wasting tire-kickers.

pending_qa.q: What is the current condition of different office market segments in Chicago?
pending_qa.r: Class A office in Chicago is performing relatively well with landlords leasing space regularly, though not as robustly as pre-COVID; the real challenge is Class B and C office, which is rough because much of Chicago's office stock was built between 1960 and 1999 and is now functionally obsolete. The solution is finding alternative paths for underperforming office—industrial conversion, multifamily, or retail—which depends heavily on zoning code understanding, municipal zoning regulations in Illinois, and site logistics; Gordon's firm has completed or is working on two or three office-to-multifamily conversion projects in the last 12 months, including one near their office.

pending_qa.q: How do underperforming office properties in Chicago find viability through adaptive reuse?
pending_qa.r: Many Class B and C office properties in Chicago were built in excellent locations—major transit corridors, great school districts, or industrial-zoned land—making them candidates for conversion to industrial, multifamily, or retail uses. Gordon recently completed an industrial conversion deal on a five-acre site in an industrial park where the current owner could break even or do modestly well despite the property's underperformance as office; determining the alternative path requires understanding Illinois municipal zoning codes and evaluating whether a site's logistics can support the proposed new use.
